extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, researchers, and journalists seeking an overview of international governmental and organizational reactions to the Jyllands-Posten Muhammad cartoons controversy
extracted.subtask_description: A compiled, encyclopedic summary of official, organizational, and public responses across countries and international bodies to the publication and republication of satirical cartoons of the Prophet Muhammad. Covers statements, resolutions, diplomatic actions, legal measures, protests, and violence arising from the controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: ICCPR relationship between freedom of religion and expression (Articles 18, 19, 20)
rubrics_metrics.description: Legally, the Government of every State party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights is bound by three articles dealing with the relationship between freedom of religion and freedom of opinion and expression, namely article 18, which protects freedom of religion, subject to such limitations as are necessary to protect public safety and order or the fundamental rights and freedoms of others (art. 18, para. 3); article 19, which protects freedom of expression and opinion, subject to certain restrictions such as 'respect of the rights or reputations of others' (art. 19, para. 3 (a)); and article 20, which states that any advocacy of national, racial or religious hatred that constitutes incitement to discrimination, hostility or violence shall be prohibited by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This passage is presented as the legal standard that states must respect: freedom of religion and expression exist but may be limited to protect public safety/order and others' rights; expression that constitutes incitement to hatred and violence must be prohibited by law.

rubrics_metrics.name: UN Secretary-General: media sensitivity and peaceful dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: The secretary-general of the UN, Kofi Annan, asked the Western media to be more sensitive in its handling of religious themes and use of peaceful dialogue after being asked by the secretary-general of the Arab League, Amr Mussa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy/ethical criterion: media covering religious themes should exercise sensitivity and promote peaceful dialogue rather than gratuitous offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: EU stance: protection of freedom of speech (Barroso)
rubrics_metrics.description: José Manuel Barroso, the president of the European Commission, supported the Danish government and said that freedom of speech cannot be compromised: 'It's better to publish too much than not to have freedom..'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative criterion promoted by EU leadership: prioritize protection of freedom of speech even when content may be offensive; implication is that publishing controversial material is preferable to restricting speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: EU trade/legal prohibition on retaliatory boycotts
rubrics_metrics.description: On January 30, 2006, the European Union said that any retaliatory boycott of Danish goods would violate world trade rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural/legal standard: economic retaliation against another state's goods in response to media publication is inconsistent with international trade rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: European Parliament resolution: condemn violence; affirm peaceful protest and absolute freedom of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: On February 15, 2006, the European Parliament accepted a resolution which condemns all violence arising from the publication of the cartoons. It stated that the EU stands in solidarity with Denmark and all other countries that have been affected by the violence. It also stated that Muslims may be offended by the cartoons and that they have the right to protest peacefully, but that the freedom of speech is absolute and may not be affected by any form of censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combined normative stance: unequivocal condemnation of violence; affirmation of right to peaceful protest by those offended; assertation that freedom of speech is absolute and should not be curtailed by censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIC five-point plan (recommendations to address Islamophobia and media practices)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OIC member states approved a five-point plan which OIC Secretary General Ekmeleddin Ihsanoglu had proposed: the plan called for the European Union to adopt legislative measures against Islamophobia; the OIC and the EU to work towards a UN Resolution on the lines of the existing UN Resolution 60/150 (Combating defamation of religions) which should prohibit defamation of all prophets and faiths; the European media to adopt a code of ethics; the United Nations to adopt an International Communication Media Order covering a definition of freedom of speech in case of religious symbols; the inclusion of a paragraph prohibiting blasphemy, defamation of religions and incitement to hatred in the text of the Human Rights Council resolution presently being negotiated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive policy package from OIC: legislative, diplomatic, and media-regulatory remedies including: (1) EU legislative measures against Islamophobia, (2) work toward a UN resolution banning defamation of prophets/faiths, (3) adoption of a European media code of ethics, (4) UN-level media order defining freedom of speech for religious symbols, (5) explicit prohibition of blasphemy/defamation/incitement in Human Rights Council texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governmental demand for apology and prevention of further occurrences
rubrics_metrics.description: Several governments lodged diplomatic protests and demanded apologies (example: Bangladesh requested the Danish government issue an apology and urged them to prevent further occurrences of 'such heinous acts').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diplomatic standard/expectation: offended states may ask for formal apologies and assurances to prevent similar publications; seen as a remedy to defuse tensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic legal action for republication or disturbance of religious peace
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples include police investigations in Finland where it is illegal to 'disturb religious peace' (police said any media that publishes the cartoons will be similarly investigated), and an editor in Belarus who reproduced cartoons being jailed for three years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical/legal consequence: domestic criminal or investigative measures may be used against publishers or republication under laws that criminalize disturbing religious peace or related offenses; media outlets face legal risk in some jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press responsibility and use of freedom with tolerance and respect
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple national leaders and officials (e.g., French foreign minister, UK Foreign Secretary Jack Straw, US statements) asserted that while freedom of the press/expression exists, it must be exercised 'in a spirit of tolerance and with respect for beliefs and religions' and 'must be coupled with press responsibility.' Jack Straw: 'There is freedom of speech, we all respect that ... But there is not any obligation to insult or to be gratuitously inflammatory.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical/style criterion for media practice: balance the right to free expression with responsibility, tolerance, and respect for religious beliefs; avoid gratuitous insult even when legal freedom exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diplomatic and economic reprisals as a form of reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Several states and subnational actors used diplomatic or economic actions — e.g., Libya recalled its ambassador and announced it would close its embassy in Denmark; Saudi Arabia withdrew its ambassadors; Kano State in Nigeria cancelled a €23 million order for Danish buses and banned Danish/Norwegian products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive standard of statecraft: diplomatic recalls, embassy closures, withdrawal of ambassadors, and trade boycotts/bans are used as state responses to offensive publications; these are political tools rather than legal adjudications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal reform to criminalize defamation of religious figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Iran amended §224-1 of its penal code to also cover defamation of Muhammed (expanding prohibitions in penal law to include defamation of the Prophet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy/legal criterion: states may respond by changing criminal law to explicitly prohibit defamation of religious figures or prophets, with potential severe penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument that freedom of speech has limits where sacred values are offended
rubrics_metrics.description: Some officials (example: Lebanese minister of foreign affairs) criticised the drawings saying that 'freedom of speech ends when sacred values are offended.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative boundary claim: a principle asserted by some actors that free speech should be limited when it offends sacred values — used to justify calls for restraint, apology, or legal action.
